newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Nordbanken CEO favours merger - paper.
newsitem.headline: Nordbanken CEO favours merger - paper.

text.p: The chief executive officer of Swedish bank Nordbanken, Hans Dalborg, said a merger between Nordbanken and rival S-E-Banken would be good, Sweden's leading newspaper reported on Monday.
"We still think that a merger with S-E-Banken is a good idea," Dalborg told Dagens Nyheter.
At the beginning of February, merger talks between the banks failed.

"From Nordbanken's point of view we thought negotiations were constructive and pleasant and that a deal would be good for shareholders, customers and others," Dalborg was quoted as saying. "We still have that vision."
He said no talks were going on at the moment.

But he said Nordbanken could need strengthening in view of more competition with stores opening banks, other companies setting up lending operations, insurance companies starting mortgage lending and card companies dealing with payments.
Furthermore, he mentioned more Nordic and Baltic market integration and the technical development, the newspaper said.
"In this situation I say that we stick to our strategy, but there are areas where Nordbanken would like to be stronger," Dalborg was quoted as saying.
"This concerns customer driven trade with interest rates and currencies and corporate finance tasks on a regional level."
"As the banks we previously cooperated with in the Nordic area now have established themselves in Sweden, we must take care of more in the future for competition reasons."
He also said that Nordbanken would utilise possibilities to strengthen itself while Swedbank and Foreningsbanken as well as Handelsbanken and Stadshypotek are busy merging, the newspaper said.
Last week, Swedbank and Foreningsbanken announced they would merge and Handelsbanken announced it finalised its 23 billion crown bid for Stadshypotek.

Dalborg was cautious when it came to 1997 earnings after Nordbanken posted a record profit of 7.4 billion crowns last year, making it the most profitable bank in Sweden for the third consecutive year.
"The interest rate fall, which gave good profits on our bond portfolio cannot be repeated. Regarding operations, pressure on interest rate margins continues to be hard," he told Dagens Nyheter.
"But the ambition is to keep up net interest income and commission levels.
The bank is prepared for the government to sell its 59 percent stake in the bank, Dalborg said.
"It is, however, quite easy to see that the market capitalisation of the state's stake has risen to much that a sale must take place in steps," he told the newspaper.
